title: Eisenhower matrix
examples: How do I decide what to do first when everything feels urgent?
Can you give me an example of something that is important but not urgent?
What is the difference between urgent and important tasks?

explain.say: Today we are learning to sort your tasks using the Eisenhower matrix.
The first step is to understand the difference between urgent and important tasks.
Next we look at importance, which relates to your long-term goals and values.
A concrete example of an important but not urgent task is planning your yearly budget.
Another example is exercising regularly; this is important for your health but not always urgent.
For a real-life example, scheduling time to learn a new professional skill is important but not immediately urgent.

faq.q: How do I know if something is truly important for my career?
faq.a: Think about where you want to be in five years. Tasks that move you toward that vision are likely important. You might also ask yourself if this task aligns with my core professional values.
asks: What matters most in my job?
How do I measure professional importance?

faq.q: If something is urgent, does that automatically mean it is important?
faq.a: No, that is a common mistake. Many things feel urgent because they demand immediate attention, but they do not actually move your goals forward. For example, answering every single email right away feels urgent but might not be important.
asks: Is urgency the same as importance?
Can something be urgent but useless?

faq.q: What should I do with tasks that are both urgent and important?
faq.a: These are your top priorities and they need your immediate, focused attention. These tasks require you to act quickly and dedicate your best energy to them first. You should schedule dedicated time for these items.

faq.q: What about tasks that are neither urgent nor important?
faq.a: These are often time-wasters or distractions. The best approach is usually to eliminate them or delegate them to someone else if possible. Do not let these consume your valuable time.
asks: How do I stop wasting time?

faq.q: Can I use this matrix for personal life goals too?
faq.a: Absolutely. This framework works for everything, not just work. You can apply it to managing your personal health, relationships, and learning goals just as easily. Treat your personal life like a project.
asks: Does this work for family life?
Is it only for work tasks?

facts: The Eisenhower matrix sorts tasks into four quadrants.
Quadrant one contains tasks that are both urgent and important.
Quadrant four contains tasks that are neither urgent nor important.
Effective time management means spending most time in the important, not urgent quadrant.

quiz.say: Calling a client about a contract renewal that is due next month is:

options.show: Do it right after a small, quick task
options.say: Do it right after a small, quick task

options.show: Ignore it until it becomes urgent
options.say: Ignore it until it becomes urgent

quiz.why: This task directly supports your long-term business goals but does not require action in the next few minutes.

wrong.0: You need to dedicate focused time to this important item, not just fit it in between other things.
wrong.2: Delegation is for tasks that are not important to you, but this task is key to your success.
wrong.3: Ignoring it will only make it more stressful when the deadline arrives.

quiz.say: Responding instantly to every incoming email notification is usually:

options.show: Schedule them for the end of the day
options.say: Schedule them for the end of the day

quiz.why: These tasks demand quick attention but do not contribute significantly to your major objectives.

wrong.0: Ignoring them might damage working relationships or miss necessary information.
wrong.1: They are often designed to feel urgent, so a small batching time is better than waiting until the end.
wrong.3: Doing them immediately stops you from working on your high-priority goals.

quiz.say: If a task is neither urgent nor important, what is the best action?

options.show: Ask a colleague to handle it
options.say: Ask a colleague to handle it

options.show: Do it quickly just to get it over with
options.say: Do it quickly just to get it over with

options.show: Save it for a slow day
options.say: Save it for a slow day

quiz.why: These tasks are distractions; removing them frees up time for more valuable work.

wrong.0: While delegation is good, if it's not important, it might be better to stop doing it altogether.
wrong.2: This wastes mental energy and time that could be used elsewhere.
wrong.3: This just postpones the distraction without solving the underlying issue.
